subtitle: Wheeze in childhood
oneLine: Clinical differentiation, severity grading, emergency bronchodilator protocol, and long-term control for childhood wheezing

chapters.title: Basics of childhood wheeze and asthma
Approach to the child with breathlessness

skill.approach.paed.rapport.expect: When approaching a breathless child, remain calm, unhurried, and examine the child on the parent lap to avoid precipitating increased agitation and worsening respiratory distress.

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Chronological age is pivotal: infants under two years presenting with their first wheezing episode typically have acute bronchiolitis, whereas children aged over three to five years with recurrent wheeze have bronchial asthma.

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Clarify whether the chief complaint is sudden-onset breathlessness, recurrent wheeze with cough, or persistent noisy breathing, and establish the exact time of onset and duration.

skill.hx.paed.presenting_complaint.expect: Elicit whether breathing difficulty is worse at night or early morning, responsiveness to inhaled bronchodilators, and presence of feeding difficulty or inability to speak.

chapters.title: Past, personal, environmental and family history

skill.hx.paed.immunisation.expect: Verify completion of primary immunisations and enquire about optional pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccines which reduce the incidence of severe viral-triggered asthma exacerbations.

skill.hx.paed.family_pedigree.expect: Construct a pedigree enquiring specifically about asthma, allergic rhinitis, and eczema in parents and siblings, which strongly increases the probability of childhood atopic asthma.

skill.hx.paed.socioeconomic.expect: Assess living conditions, kitchen ventilation, domestic tobacco and bidi smoke, and biomass fuel use (chulha), which serve as significant environmental triggers for recurrent wheezing.

chapters.title: General physical examination and distress signs

skill.gen.paed.appearance.expect: Observe the child posture and alertness from a distance: sitting upright or in the tripod position and agitated or drowsy indicates severe respiratory distress.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.expect: Measure respiratory rate over a full 60 seconds; tachypnoea, tachycardia, and room-air SpO2 <92% signify a severe exacerbation.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.expect: Inspect the tongue and buccal mucous membranes for central cyanosis, an emergency warning sign of life-threatening hypoxaemia.

skill.gen.paed.clubbing.expect: Digital clubbing is never a feature of asthma; its presence points towards cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, or cyanotic congenital heart disease.

skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.expect: Look for hyperinflation of the chest, intercostal and subcostal indrawing, suprasternal retraction, and nasal flaring indicating high work of breathing.

skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.expect: Listen for prolonged expiration and diffuse polyphonic wheezes; a silent chest with markedly reduced breath sounds indicates impending respiratory failure.

skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.expect: Distinguish between musical expiratory wheezing (intrathoracic airway narrowing), inspiratory stridor (upper airway obstruction), and expiratory grunting (alveolar collapse).

chapters.title: Putting the wheezing child picture together

skill.proc.paed.pefr.expect: In children over five years, measure PEFR to grade severity objectively: <50% of predicted represents the red zone (severe exacerbation) and <33% signals life-threatening asthma.

skill.ix.paed.cxr_approach.expect: Chest radiography is not routine; reserve for suspected pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, marked asymmetry, or failure to improve with intensive bronchodilators.

skill.proc.paed.inhaler_devices.expect: Prescribe a metered-dose inhaler with a valve-holding spacer and face mask for children under 4 years, or with a mouthpiece for older children; verify seal and slow tidal breathing.

skill.present.case.expect: Present the case structured around triage severity, physiological vital signs, underlying atopic phenotype, and acute response to emergency bronchodilators.

stations.title: Assess and manage a child with acute severe asthma
stations.task: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the emergency triage with severe breathlessness and audible wheeze. Assess her respiratory distress, identify emergency red flags, determine her asthma severity, and outline immediate bronchodilator and oxygen therapy.
examinerQuestions: What clinical signs indicate acute severe or life-threatening asthma rather than a mild exacerbation?
The child speaks in single words, has marked subcostal indrawing, and oxygen saturation is 90% on room air. What is your immediate management in the first 15 to 30 minutes?
If the chest auscultation reveals markedly reduced breath sounds with no wheeze, how do you interpret this finding and what action do you take?

stations.title: Demonstrate MDI with spacer and formulate a long-term asthma plan
stations.task: An 8-year-old boy with frequent nocturnal cough and exertional wheeze is being started on regular preventer therapy. Demonstrate the correct technique of using a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer device, assess PEFR, and counsel the mother on trigger avoidance.
examinerQuestions: Demonstrate and explain the step-by-step sequence of using a metered-dose inhaler with a valve-holding spacer in this 8-year-old child.
How would you explain the PEFR traffic light zones (green, yellow, red) to the mother, and what action should she take in the red zone?
Why is mouth rinsing essential after using an inhaled corticosteroid, and what common local adverse effect does it prevent?

skill.asthma.child.basics.title: What childhood wheezing, asthma, and bronchiolitis are
skill.asthma.child.basics.why: Understanding the triphasic pathophysiology of airway narrowing, bronchial smooth muscle constriction, mucosal inflammation with oedema, and intraluminal mucus plugging, explains why treatment requires both rapid-acting bronchodilators and anti-inflammatory corticosteroids.

teach.heading: The anatomical and physiological basis of paediatric wheeze
teach.body:
Wheezing is a continuous, high-pitched, musical adventitious lung sound generated during expiration when airflow passes through narrowed or compressed intrathoracic airways.

In young children, small airway caliber, high peripheral airway resistance, and compliant chest wall dynamics make them exceptionally prone to significant airflow limitation in response to minimal mucosal swelling or smooth muscle constriction.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of bronchial asthma
teach.body:
Childhood asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the conducting airways driven by complex immune activation.

Airway hyperresponsiveness to non-specific stimuli leads to recurrent episodes of widespread, variable airflow obstruction. Dynamic hyperinflation increases end-expiratory lung volume, flattening the diaphragms and increasing the mechanical work of breathing.

teach.heading: Pathophysiology of acute bronchiolitis
teach.body:
Acute bronchiolitis is a self-limiting viral infection of the lower respiratory tract, predominantly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) in infants under two years.

Viral invasion of bronchiolar epithelial cells leads to necrosis, ciliary disruption, peribronchiolar lymphocytic infiltration, and submucosal oedema. Plugs of desquamated epithelial debris and dense mucus occlude the bronchioles, causing patchy atelectasis and air trapping.

probes.q: What triad of pathological changes produces airway narrowing during an acute paediatric asthma attack?
probes.a: Bronchial smooth muscle bronchospasm, airway mucosal inflammation with oedema, and hypersecretion of thick mucus forming intraluminal plugs.

probes.q: Why are infants anatomically more predisposed to severe airflow obstruction during lower respiratory tract infections?
probes.a: Infants have smaller baseline airway diameters, increased peripheral airway resistance, higher compliant chest wall dynamics, and fewer collateral ventilatory channels such as the pores of Kohn.

rubric.text: Explains smooth muscle spasm, mucosal oedema, and mucus plugging
Outlines infant airway caliber and chest wall compliance peculiarities
Differentiates epithelial necrosis in bronchiolitis from eosinophilic asthma

skill.asthma.child.findings.title: The paediatric wheeze picture: physical signs and physiological strain
skill.asthma.child.findings.why: Correlating work of breathing, chest wall retractions, respiratory rate, and chest auscultation with airflow dynamics enables the clinician to detect deteriorating ventilation before overt respiratory arrest supervenes.

teach.heading: Work of breathing and dynamic retractions
teach.body:
Increased respiratory effort in an obstructed child manifests as chest wall recessions. Subcostal and intercostal indrawing reflect the large negative intrathoracic pressures generated during inspiration against narrow airways.

Suprasternal and supraclavicular retractions indicate recruitment of accessory neck muscles, while sternocleidomastoid contraction and head bobbing in younger infants denote severe physiological exhaustion.

teach.heading: Auscultation dynamics and the danger of the silent chest
teach.body:
Auscultation in mild to moderate asthma reveals prolonged expiration with diffuse, bilateral, high-pitched polyphonic expiratory rhonchi.

Critically, when airway obstruction becomes extreme, air movement diminishes to such low velocities that wheezes disappear completely. A silent chest with poor air entry is an ominous emergency sign of impending respiratory failure, not a sign of recovery.

probes.q: Why is a silent chest on auscultation in a severely dyspnoeic child a medical emergency?
probes.a: A silent chest indicates profound airway obstruction where airflow velocity is insufficient even to produce wheezing, heralding respiratory muscle exhaustion and imminent asphyxial arrest.

probes.q: Explain why expiration is prolonged in intrathoracic small-airway obstruction.
probes.a: Intrathoracic positive pressure generated during expiration compresses diseased airways from the outside, further narrowing bronchiolar lumina and markedly lengthening the time required for passive lung emptying.

rubric.text: Grades severity of retractions from subcostal to suprasternal and head bobbing
Recognises the silent chest as critical airflow limitation
Explains dynamic compression producing prolonged expiratory phase

skill.asthma.child.summary.title: Synthesising the clinical summary in the wheezing child
skill.asthma.child.summary.why: A disciplined clinical summary succinctly unifies age, symptom pattern, atopic markers, vital sign derangements, and acute distress severity into a coherent diagnostic formulation that directs emergency care.

teach.heading: Framework for the paediatric respiratory summary
teach.body:
A concise clinical summary should follow a five-part clinical construct: age and gender, chief complaint with exact duration, underlying phenotype (episodic viral wheeze, multiple-trigger wheeze, or infant bronchiolitis), key positive and negative physical signs, and functional severity grading.

Synthesising these elements distinguishes acute bronchospasm needing immediate bronchodilators from upper airway or parenchymal disorders.

teach.heading: Synthesising severity and physiological stability
teach.body:
Always conclude the summary by categorising functional impairment: talkability (whether speaking in words, phrases, or unable to speak), feeding ability, mental status (calm, agitated, or drowsy), and room-air pulse oximetry.

Stating physiological stability immediately clarifies whether the child can be managed in an outpatient observation bay or requires high-dependency paediatric intensive care resuscitation.

probes.q: What five components should be synthesised in the bedside summary of a wheezing child?
probes.a: Child age and sex, duration of breathlessness, phenotypic pattern of wheeze with atopic background, vital sign derangements and retractions, and current severity grade.

probes.q: In an infant under twelve months, what clinical details in the summary confirm acute bronchiolitis over asthma?
probes.a: First episode of acute wheeze, age under twelve months, a preceding two to three day coryzal upper respiratory prodrome, fine inspiratory crackles alongside wheeze, and lack of personal atopic history.

rubric.text: Constructs a concise summary integrating age, history, and severity
Explicitly states talkability, retractions, and oximetry
Highlights features distinguishing infant bronchiolitis from asthma

skill.asthma.child.differential.title: Differential diagnosis of paediatric wheezing and small-airway obstruction
skill.asthma.child.differential.why: Recognising that not every wheezing child has asthma prevents inappropriate reliance on bronchodilators in conditions such as foreign body aspiration, acute viral bronchiolitis, vascular rings, or cystic fibrosis.

teach.heading: Acute wheezing mimics in toddlers and children
teach.body:
Sudden onset of unheralded wheezing or persistent unilateral wheeze in a previously healthy toddler strongly suggests tracheobronchial foreign body aspiration.

Foreign bodies (such as peanuts, seeds, or small toy parts) produce localized air trapping or atelectasis, lack reversibility with bronchodilators, and show focal hyperinflation on inspiratory-expiratory chest radiographs.

Viral croup causes harsh inspiratory stridor with barking cough rather than pure expiratory wheeze.

teach.heading: Chronic and recurrent wheezing differentials
teach.body:
Persistent or unremitting wheeze from early infancy suggests congenital structural anomalies, including vascular rings, tracheobronchomalacia, or external airway compression by mediastinal lymphadenopathy.

Cystic fibrosis and primary ciliary dyskinesia present with recurrent wet cough, purulent sputum, failure to thrive, and digital clubbing, which are conspicuously absent in uncomplicated childhood asthma.

teach.heading: Differential table of childhood wheeze

probes.q: What clinical features distinguish tracheobronchial foreign body aspiration from an acute asthma exacerbation?
probes.a: Sudden onset of choking or coughing while eating or playing, persistent unilateral wheeze, lack of response to bronchodilators, and focal hyperinflation or atelectasis on chest radiograph.

probes.q: Why should digital clubbing in a wheezing child prompt investigation beyond bronchial asthma?
probes.a: Uncomplicated asthma never causes digital clubbing. Its presence indicates chronic suppurative lung disease such as cystic fibrosis, bronchiectasis, or cyanotic congenital heart disease.

rubric.text: Identifies unilateral wheeze and sudden choking in foreign body aspiration
Differentiates infant bronchiolitis from recurrent asthma
Screens for vascular rings, tracheomalacia, and cystic fibrosis

skill.ix.asthma.child.workup.title: Diagnostic workup, physiological monitoring, and imaging in paediatric asthma
skill.ix.asthma.child.workup.why: Targeted investigations confirm variable airflow obstruction, document acute hypoxaemia and hypercapnia, and exclude complications such as pneumothorax or lobar consolidation without ordering indiscriminate tests.

teach.heading: Physiological monitoring: pulse oximetry and blood gas analysis
teach.body:
Continuous pulse oximetry is the initial non-invasive investigation in all acute presentations; an oxygen saturation below 92% on ambient air flags severe exacerbation.

Blood gas analysis (capillary or venous) is indicated when a child shows severe respiratory distress or exhaustion.

Early tachypnoea washes out carbon dioxide, producing hypocapnia. A normalising or elevated PaCO2 (38 to 42 mmHg or higher) in a tiring child is an ominous warning of impending respiratory failure.

teach.heading: Spirometry and peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
teach.body:
In children over five years, peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) provides an objective measurement of airflow limitation.

Readings are interpreted using traffic-light zones: green (>80% predicted), yellow (50-80%), and red (<50%). A value below 33% marks life-threatening asthma.

In outpatient evaluation, formal spirometry demonstrating an FEV1 increase of >=12% after inhaled salbutamol confirms reversible bronchoconstriction.

teach.heading: Chest radiography indications and electrolyte monitoring
teach.body:
Routine chest radiography is not recommended in standard asthma exacerbations. Radiographs are reserved for suspected pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, severe unilateral chest signs, lobar collapse, or failure to respond to intensive bronchodilator therapy.

Repeated or high-dose beta-2 agonist therapy drives potassium into cells, mandating serum electrolyte monitoring to prevent clinically significant hypokalaemia.

probes.q: How should a normal PaCO2 value on blood gas be interpreted in a child with severe tachypnoea and asthma exacerbation?
probes.a: It is an ominous warning sign of impending respiratory failure and respiratory muscle exhaustion, because hyperventilation should normally produce hypocapnia.

probes.q: What are the specific clinical indications for ordering a chest radiograph in acute childhood asthma?
probes.a: Suspected pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema, severe unilateral chest findings, fever with suspected pneumonia, or failure to respond to initial bronchodilator therapy.

rubric.text: Interprets oximetry cutoffs and pseudonormal PaCO2 on blood gas
Utilises PEFR zones and spirometric reversibility criteria
Applies restrictive criteria for chest radiography and monitors potassium

skill.asthma.child.diagnosis.title: Severity classification and clinical grading of acute asthma exacerbations
skill.asthma.child.diagnosis.why: Accurate clinical grading into mild, moderate, severe, and life-threatening exacerbations dictates the urgency of emergency interventions, frequency of bronchodilators, systemic steroid dosing, and PICU escalation.

teach.heading: Grading acute asthma severity: clinical criteria
teach.body:
Severity of an acute exacerbation is assessed by integrating mental status, speech capability, respiratory rate, retraction intensity, and room-air oxygen saturation.

Mild exacerbations feature minor tachypnoea, ability to talk in sentences, and SpO2 >95%.

Moderate exacerbations present with talk in phrases, visible intercostal indrawing, and SpO2 92-95%.

Severe attacks feature speaking in single words, marked sternal retractions, and SpO2 <92%.

teach.heading: Life-threatening asthma features and the CHEST mnemonic
teach.body:
Life-threatening asthma constitutes an immediate medical emergency requiring intensive resuscitation.

The CHEST mnemonic highlights five cardinal danger signs: C for cyanosis, confusion, or coma; H for hypotension; E for exhaustion; S for silent chest with absent air entry; and T for threatening PEFR under 33% of predicted.

Any single feature in this category mandates immediate emergency escalation.

teach.heading: Summary severity grading matrix

probes.q: List three clinical signs that classify a paediatric asthma exacerbation as severe rather than moderate.
probes.a: Inability to speak in sentences (speaking in single words), marked subcostal and suprasternal retractions, agitation, and room-air oxygen saturation below 92%.

probes.q: What five life-threatening features are captured by the CHEST mnemonic in acute childhood asthma?
probes.a: Cyanosis or confusion or coma, hypotension, exhaustion, silent chest, and threatening PEFR under 33 percent of predicted.

rubric.text: Integrates speech, retractions, respiratory rate, and SpO2
Applies the CHEST mnemonic for life-threatening asthma
Directs appropriate triage placement based on clinical severity

skill.tx.asthma.child.acute.title: Emergency management of acute asthma exacerbation and status asthmaticus
skill.tx.asthma.child.acute.why: A standardised emergency sequence of humidified oxygen, frequent inhaled short-acting beta-agonists, anticholinergic synergy, early systemic steroids, and intravenous magnesium sulfate reverses acute bronchospasm, reduces hospitalisation, and prevents fatal asphyxiation.
skill.tx.asthma.child.acute.dosingNote: Dosing note: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses quoted are standard reference doses from cited clinical guidelines (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and Indian Academy of Pediatrics). Always verify with local hospital protocols.

teach.heading: Oxygen therapy and inhaled bronchodilators
teach.body:
First-line emergency intervention requires high-flow humidified oxygen via face mask or nasal prongs to maintain target SpO2 between 94% and 98%.

Inhaled salbutamol (short-acting beta-2 agonist) is administered immediately: 4 to 10 puffs via metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, or nebulised at 2.5 mg (under 5 years) or 5 mg (5 years and older), repeated every 20 minutes for the first hour.

In severe exacerbations, inhaled ipratropium bromide (250 micrograms nebulised, or 4 puffs of 20 micrograms via spacer) is added to salbutamol every 20 minutes for the first hour to produce synergistic bronchodilatation.

teach.heading: Systemic corticosteroids and second-line intravenous therapies
teach.body:
Systemic corticosteroids must be administered within the first hour of presentation to resolve mucosal inflammation: oral prednisolone 1 to 2 mg/kg (maximum 40 mg in children), or intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg (maximum 100 mg) if the child cannot swallow or is vomiting.

For refractory acute severe asthma unresponsive to initial inhaled bronchodilators, intravenous magnesium sulfate (40 to 50 mg/kg infused over 20 to 30 minutes, maximum 2 g) promotes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation by inhibiting calcium influx.

teach.heading: Emergency escalation and intensive care criteria
teach.body:
If the child shows signs of life-threatening asthma (CHEST criteria: cyanosis, confusion, exhaustion, silent chest, or PEFR <33%), immediate paediatric intensive care consultation is mandatory.

Advanced medical options include continuous nebulised salbutamol, intravenous salbutamol infusion, or intravenous aminophylline with continuous cardiac monitoring.

Endotracheal intubation in asthma carries high risks of severe air trapping and pneumothorax, and is reserved for respiratory arrest or coma using lung-protective ventilation.

probes.q: Why should systemic corticosteroids be administered within the first hour of arrival during an acute asthma exacerbation?
probes.a: Early administration suppresses acute airway mucosal inflammation, reduces hospitalisation rates, speeds clinical recovery, and prevents rebound exacerbations.

probes.q: What is the mechanism of action and standard dose of intravenous magnesium sulfate in severe acute paediatric asthma?
probes.a: It acts as a calcium channel antagonist to relax bronchial smooth muscle, administered at 40 to 50 mg/kg infused over twenty to thirty minutes up to a maximum of 2 grams.

rubric.text: Initiates oxygen and repeated inhaled salbutamol with ipratropium
Administers systemic corticosteroids within the first hour
Escalates to intravenous magnesium sulfate and PICU when refractory

skill.tx.asthma.child.chronic.title: Long-term controller therapy, step-up management, and asthma action plans
skill.tx.asthma.child.chronic.why: Daily maintenance with low-dose inhaled corticosteroids prevents chronic airway remodeling, eliminates nocturnal symptoms, maintains normal physical activity, and minimises future exacerbation risk.
skill.tx.asthma.child.chronic.dosingNote: Dosing note: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses quoted are standard reference doses from cited clinical guidelines (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and Indian Academy of Pediatrics). Always verify with local hospital protocols.

teach.heading: Stepwise controller therapy in children
teach.body:
Long-term management follows stepwise escalation based on symptom frequency and exacerbation risk.

Step 1 (infrequent symptoms) requires an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing approach: taking a low-dose ICS whenever SABA is inhaled (or as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol where approved for ages 6 to 11). As-needed SABA alone without an ICS is no longer recommended because SABA monotherapy increases severe exacerbation risk.

Step 2 (symptoms twice a month or more, or waking with asthma) introduces regular daily low-dose ICS (such as budesonide 100 to 200 micrograms daily or fluticasone propionate) as the preferred controller. Oral montelukast is an alternative controller, but clinicians must warn parents of its serious neuropsychiatric boxed warning (nightmares, agitation, insomnia, and mood changes) and stop the drug if behavioural symptoms occur.

Step 3 escalates to a paediatric low-dose ICS-LABA combination, respecting molecule-specific minimum age approvals (such as salmeterol from 4 years or formoterol from 6 years), or alternatively increases to medium-dose ICS.

teach.heading: Device selection, technique verification, and mouth care
teach.body:
Drug delivery efficiency depends on matching the device to the child age and inspiratory capability: children under four years require a pressurized metered-dose inhaler (pMDI) with a valved holding chamber spacer and closely fitted face mask.

Children aged four to twelve years use a pMDI with a mouthpiece spacer; breath-actuated dry powder inhalers (DPIs) can also be used effectively from above four to five years in children able to generate sufficient inspiratory flow. Using a pMDI alone without a spacer is reserved for older children over twelve years who demonstrate reliable hand-breath coordination.

Every consultation must directly observe inhaler technique and verify device seal integrity. Rinsing the mouth with water and spitting after inhaled corticosteroids prevents local oropharyngeal candidiasis and dysphonia.

teach.heading: The written asthma action plan and trigger avoidance
teach.body:
Every family must receive an individualised written asthma action plan outlining three distinct zones: green zone for daily preventer use and normal activity when well; yellow zone for worsening symptoms or wheeze requiring increased reliever puffs and prompt medical contact, without unmonitored home oral steroid starts; and red zone for emergency warning signs requiring immediate hospital presentation.

Oral corticosteroids in children must not be started routinely at home by families without clinician evaluation. Action plans instruct increasing inhaled bronchodilator frequency in the yellow zone and contacting health services promptly if symptoms do not rapidly improve, reserving systemic steroids for medical assessment.

Environmental control includes eliminating domestic tobacco and bidi smoke, substituting biomass fuel with clean LPG, avoiding burning incense or mosquito coils, and regularly washing bedsheets in hot water to reduce dust mite allergens.

probes.q: Why is an inhaler spacer device essential when administering a metered-dose inhaler to a school-age child?
probes.a: The spacer slows aerosol particle velocity and eliminates the need for press-and-breathe hand-lung coordination, reducing oropharyngeal deposition and dramatically increasing drug delivery to the lower airways.

probes.q: What three action zones must be detailed in a paediatric written asthma action plan?
probes.a: Green zone for daily routine maintenance when well, yellow zone for early flare-up symptoms requiring increased reliever use and prompt medical contact, and red zone for severe danger signs requiring emergency hospital presentation.

rubric.text: Outlines stepwise controller escalation with ICS-containing therapy from Step 1 onwards
Selects age-appropriate inhaler device with spacer and counsels on mouth rinsing
Constructs a three-zone written asthma action plan and environmental plan

skill.tx.bronchiolitis.supportive.title: Evidence-based supportive management of acute viral bronchiolitis
skill.tx.bronchiolitis.supportive.why: Avoiding routine bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, and antibiotics in acute infant bronchiolitis prevents therapeutic harm while focusing clinical efforts on hydration, oxygenation, and respiratory monitoring.
skill.tx.bronchiolitis.supportive.dosingNote: Dosing note: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses quoted are standard reference doses from cited clinical guidelines (Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics and Indian Academy of Pediatrics). Always verify with local hospital protocols.

teach.heading: The supportive care paradigm in infant bronchiolitis
teach.body:
Acute viral bronchiolitis is self-limiting and driven by viral epithelial sloughing and luminal mucus obstruction rather than reversible smooth muscle bronchospasm.

Large international randomized clinical trials have conclusively demonstrated that bronchodilators (salbutamol), systemic corticosteroids, and montelukast do not shorten hospital stay, reduce admission rates, or accelerate resolution.

Routine pharmacotherapy is therefore not recommended, avoiding tachycardia and systemic side effects.

teach.heading: Hydration, gentle suction, and oxygen delivery
teach.body:
Management centres on three supportive pillars: oxygenation, hydration, and gentle nasal clearance.

Humidified oxygen is administered if SpO2 persistently falls below 90% to 92%.

Small, frequent fractionated oral feeds reduce aspiration risk in tachypnoeic infants; if intake falls below 50% of maintenance or the infant tires, nasogastric feeding or isotonic intravenous maintenance fluids (such as 0.9% saline with 5% dextrose) are instituted.

Superficial nasal suctioning clears thick secretions before feeding.

teach.heading: Hospital admission and discharge criteria
teach.body:
Indications for hospital admission in bronchiolitis include persistent room-air SpO2 <92%, moderate to severe chest retractions, respiratory rate >60 to 70 breaths/min, poor oral feeding (<50% normal), apnoea episodes, or young age under six to twelve weeks.

Discharge is safe once the infant maintains SpO2 >=92% on ambient air for at least 12 hours, feeds adequately without respiratory distress, and parents are counseled on danger signs.

probes.q: Why are systemic corticosteroids and inhaled salbutamol not routinely recommended for acute bronchiolitis in infants?
probes.a: Airway obstruction in bronchiolitis is caused by epithelial necrosis and mucus plugs rather than smooth muscle bronchospasm, and randomized trials show no benefit in reducing admissions or length of stay.

probes.q: State three clinical criteria that mandate hospital admission for an infant with acute bronchiolitis.
probes.a: Oxygen saturation below 92% on room air, marked chest indrawing with grunting, inability to feed adequately (less than 50% maintenance), and any documented apnoeic episode.

rubric.text: Prioritises oxygen, hydration, and minimal handling over unnecessary drugs
Justifies withholding routine bronchodilators, steroids, and antibiotics
Applies objective criteria for hospital admission and discharge

cases.title: A 6-year-old girl with acute breathlessness and audible wheeze
cases.opening: Doctor, my 6-year-old daughter Aanya has been coughing and wheezing since yesterday evening. Tonight she woke up struggling to breathe, her chest is pulling in deeply, and she can only speak two or three words at a time. Her blue inhaler did not help like it usually does!
cases.fallback: The mother looks anxious and holds Aanya upright on her lap. Aanya is sitting forward, breathing rapidly with audible expiratory wheeze and marked suprasternal indrawing.

patient.name: Aanya Sharma
patient.residence: Semi-urban locality near an industrial bypass road, Jaipur, Rajasthan; lives in a pucca house with parents and paternal grandparents

cues: what brought you to the hospital
presenting.reply: She developed severe breathlessness and a loud whistling chest sound since yesterday evening. It became much worse tonight around midnight, and she cannot lie flat.

cough_symptoms.reply: She has a dry, hacking, tight cough that worsens during the night and early morning. It started two days ago after she returned from school.

wheeze_character.reply: It sounds like a continuous high-pitched musical whistle whenever she breathes out. You can hear it even without putting your ear to her chest.

triggers_exposure.reply: She was playing outside on Thursday evening during a sudden dusty windstorm. The weather has also turned quite chilly over the past two days.

past_episodes.reply: She has had three similar episodes of wheezing over the last twelve months, usually following a common cold. She was admitted to the ward once last winter for two days.

medication_history.reply: Her doctor previously gave her a blue salbutamol inhaler with a plastic spacer chamber. At home tonight we gave her two puffs twice, but it only helped for ten minutes.

atopic_history.reply: As a baby she had red itchy dry patches on her cheeks and elbow creases that needed moisturising creams. She also gets frequent bouts of morning sneezing with clear watery nasal discharge.

family_atopy.reply: Her father has suffered from bronchial asthma since his teenage years and uses an inhaler regularly. Her paternal aunt has chronic allergic skin rashes.

feeding_activity.reply: She refused dinner tonight and could only take small sips of warm water. She cannot speak a full sentence and pauses after every two or three words to catch her breath.

fever_infection.reply: She had a mild low-grade fever of around 99 F and a clear runny nose two days ago, but she has not felt burning hot and has had no chills.

foreign_body.reply: No, there was definitely no sudden episode of choking, coughing fits while eating nuts, or playing with small toy beads or coins.

birth_neonatal.reply: She was born at full term through a normal hospital delivery, cried vigorously at birth, weighed 2.9 kg, and required no nursery admission or oxygen.

immunisation_history.reply: She has received all primary vaccinations up to age five as per the national schedule. She received her last booster at five years, but has never received the annual flu vaccine.

developmental_milestones.reply: She walked before one year, speaks fluently in Hindi and English, attends regular school, and performs well academically.

environmental_housing.reply: We cook using LPG gas cylinders. However, her grandfather smokes bidis in the open courtyard, and our house is close to an unpaved road with heavy vehicular dust.

urinary_bowel.reply: She passed urine three hours ago and has had no diarrhoea or vomiting.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.finding: Alert but visibly distressed, sitting upright in the tripod position, unable to speak in complete sentences without pausing for breath.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.finding: Heart rate 138 beats per minute (tachycardia for age), respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute with prolonged expiration, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, temperature 37.1 C, oxygen saturation 91% on room air.

skill.gen.paed.cyanosis.finding: No central or peripheral cyanosis visible on the tongue, oral mucosa, or nail beds; capillary refill time is brisk at 1.5 seconds.

skill.gen.paed.clubbing.finding: No digital clubbing or fluctuation of the nail beds (normal profile angle preserved).

skill.gen.paed.hydration.finding: Warm extremities, tears present when crying, moist buccal mucosa, normal skin turgor with instantaneous recoil.

skill.exam.paed.resp.inspection.finding: Hyperinflated chest appearance with increased anteroposterior diameter; prominent accessory muscle use with marked intercostal and subcostal indrawing, suprasternal retraction, and mild alae nasi flaring.

skill.exam.paed.resp.palpation.finding: Trachea is strictly central in the suprasternal notch; symmetrical bilateral chest expansion with no chest wall tenderness or palpable crepitus.

skill.exam.paed.resp.percussion.finding: Resonant to hyperresonant percussion note bilaterally throughout all lung zones, with physiological downward displacement of liver dullness to the 6th intercostal space.

skill.exam.paed.resp.auscultation.finding: Markedly prolonged expiratory phase with widespread bilateral polyphonic high-pitched expiratory rhonchi and scattered inspiratory wheezes; vesicular breath sounds preserved without focal bronchial breathing.

skill.exam.paed.resp.distress_grunt.finding: Audible expiratory wheeze without stethoscope; no inspiratory stridor and no expiratory grunting.

oximetry.label: Continuous pulse oximetry
oximetry.result: SpO2 91% on room air, improving to 96% with supplemental oxygen via face mask at 4 L/min.
oximetry.note: Confirms acute hypoxaemia requiring immediate controlled oxygen therapy.

pefr.label: Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR)
pefr.result: Pre-bronchodilator PEFR 110 L/min (predicted for height 115 cm is 230 L/min; 48% of predicted, placing the child in the Red Zone).
pefr.note: Demonstrates severe airflow limitation; repeat 20 minutes post-bronchodilator shows rise to 160 L/min (>45% improvement).

chest_xray.label: Chest Radiograph (PA view)
chest_xray.result: Bilateral pulmonary hyperinflation with flattened diaphragms and increased retrosternal lucency; prominent bronchovascular markings without focal parenchymal consolidation, pneumothorax, or pneumomediastinum.
chest_xray.note: Excludes pneumothorax, lobar collapse, and consolidation; not routinely indicated at initial presentation unless complications or poor bronchodilator response occur.

blood_gas.label: Capillary / Venous Blood Gas
blood_gas.result: pH 7.36, PaCO2 40 mmHg, PaO2 60 mmHg on room air, HCO3- 22 mEq/L, base excess -2 mEq/L.
blood_gas.note: A pseudonormal PaCO2 of 40 mmHg in a child with marked tachypnoea (respiratory rate 46/min) demonstrates failing hyperventilation and impending respiratory muscle exhaustion.

complete_blood_count.label: Complete Blood Count and Absolute Eosinophil Count
complete_blood_count.result: Haemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, Total Leukocyte Count 9,200/uL with 58% neutrophils, 32% lymphocytes, 8% eosinophils; Absolute Eosinophil Count 736/uL.
complete_blood_count.note: Peripheral eosinophilia supports an underlying atopic diathesis; no leukocytosis with toxic granules.

differentialModel.answer: Acute severe asthma exacerbation in a child with bronchial asthma. Key differentials include acute bronchiolitis (in infants), community-acquired pneumonia with wheeze, foreign body aspiration, viral croup, and pneumothorax.

diagnosis.answer: Acute severe asthma exacerbation in a 6-year-old child with underlying bronchial asthma.

managementModel.answer: Immediate high-flow humidified oxygen to maintain SpO2 94-98%, back-to-back inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist (salbutamol) with inhaled ipratropium via MDI and spacer or nebulisation, early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or intravenous hydrocortisone), intravenous magnesium sulfate for poor response, continuous clinical and oximetry monitoring, and discharge planning with written action plan and inhaled corticosteroid controller.

teachingPoints: In acute severe paediatric asthma, clinical assessment of the work of breathing, accessory muscle use, ability to speak, and mental status is more vital than auscultatory loudness, as a silent chest indicates critical, life-threatening airflow obstruction.

Early in severe acute asthma, hyperventilation typically drives PaCO2 down (hypocapnia). A normal PaCO2 (38-42 mmHg) or rising PaCO2 in a struggling, exhausted child is an ominous warning of impending respiratory failure.

Metered-dose inhalers (MDI) coupled with a valved holding chamber and spacer deliver bronchodilators with equal or superior pulmonary deposition compared to jet nebulisers in mild-to-moderate exacerbations, with fewer systemic adverse effects.

Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 1-2 mg/kg/day, maximum 40 mg, or intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg) must be administered early within the first hour of emergency presentation to resolve airway mucosal inflammation and reduce hospitalisation.

Every child discharged after an acute asthma exacerbation requires a verified inhaler technique check, initiation or step-up of inhaled corticosteroid preventer therapy, identification and mitigation of domestic triggers, and a clear written asthma action plan.
